newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Iscor looking at Australian nickel.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Iscor looking at Australian nickel.

text.p: South African steel giant Iscor Ltd's mining division is looking at moving into the nickel market as part of its drive to become a major mining company, a company official said Friday.

In the past Iscor has mainly mined coal and iron ore to feed its steel works. But in recent years, the company diversified its mining operations to include mineral sands mining in Australia and several exploration projects in Africa.
The company predominantly focused on gold, copper, iron ore and nickel, and to a lesser extent coal and zinc in its new exploration and mining efforts.
"Like everybody else we would like to grow and then you look around. Anything that can make money in a country that we can handle we will look at.
"That will be outside what we traditionally mine, and nickel is one of those," Iscor global scouting manager Van der Spuy Brink told Reuters.
Brink said Iscor's steel division would be a major consumer of nickel.
"Obviously that gives you some strength in that particular market and that particular commodity, so obviously we would be interested," he said in a telephone interview.
Brink said Iscor was looking at promising deposits in Australia and New Caledonia although the company would prefer to source its nickel from Africa.
"There are promising deposits we are looking at, but it is years from mining."
"We prefer to do it in Africa, our hunting ground is Africa," Brink said.
Iscor recently converted its Pretoria steel plant to stainless steel manufacturing and would need around 8,000 to 10,000 tonnes of nickel in the plant's first year of operation.
This will increase to about 14,000 tonnes in its second year.
Iscor said in April it had secured a long-term contract worth $112 million a year with an international trader to supply the Pretoria plant with nickel.

Brink said if Iscor's mining division could establish a nickel mine and deliver the metal to its Pretoria and Durban plants at a competitive price, the stainless steel plants would be potential customers.
"If we can get a mine going and transport the nickel to Pretoria and Durban at a competitive price, yes it will be used," he said.
But he stressed that Iscor will concentrate its mining efforts on Sub-Saharan Africa.
The company qualified and tendered to develop the giant Tenke Fungurume copper deposit in Zaire's southern Shaba province. But its bid failed.
"We have not got the bid at this point but...we are very active up there (in Zaire)," Brink said.

Mining analysts say Zaire is potentially one of the richest mineral resource regions in the world but political and economic chaos have prevented foreign mining companies from investing. --Johannesburg newsroom, +27-11 482 1003
